section.title: Living to Please God
section.sectionRationale: Turning from thanksgiving to exhortation, Paul urges the church to excel in a life that pleases God. He grounds it in God's will for their sanctification: sexual purity that honors God and neighbor, brotherly love that overflows, and quiet, honest, diligent living that commends the gospel to outsiders.
section.thesis: God's will for His people is their sanctification: to abandon the impurity of the surrounding world for sexual holiness that honors God and does not wrong others, and to grow in brotherly love and quiet, industrious living, because the God who calls them gives them His Holy Spirit.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the call to please God more and more; sanctification in sexual purity as God's will, backed by His judgment and His Spirit; and love, quiet living, and honest work that adorn the faith before outsiders.

verses.text: Finally, brothers, we ask and encourage you in the Lord Jesus to live in a way that is {{aresko|pleasing}} to God, just as you have received from us. This is how you already live, so you should do so all the more.
For you know the instructions we gave you by the authority of the Lord Jesus.

units.label: Sanctification in sexual purity
units.note: God's will, honoring God and neighbor

verses.text: For it is God's will that you should be holy: You must abstain from {{porneia|sexual immorality}};
each of you must know how to control his own {{skeuos|body}} in {{hagiasmos|holiness}} and honor,
not in lustful {{epithymia|passion}} like the Gentiles who do not know God;
and no one should ever violate or exploit his brother in this regard, because the Lord will avenge all such acts, as we have already told you and solemnly warned you.
For God has not called us to {{akatharsia|impurity}}, but to holiness.
Anyone, then, who rejects this command does not reject man but God, the very One who gives you His {{pneuma|Holy Spirit}}.

units.label: Love, quiet living, and honest work

verses.text: Now about brotherly love, you do not need anyone to write to you, because you yourselves have been taught by God to {{philadelphia|love}} one another.
And you are indeed showing this love to all the brothers throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers, to excel more and more
and to aspire to live {{hesychazo|quietly}}, to attend to your own matters, and to work with your own hands, as we instructed you.
Then you will behave properly toward outsiders, without being dependent on anyone.

aresko.gloss: To please, to be acceptable to. Paul urges the church to live so as to please God, which becomes the governing aim of Christian conduct. Pleasing God is not anxious performance to earn favor but the glad response of those already loved and called, growing more and more into a life that delights Him.

porneia.gloss: Sexual immorality, a broad term for sexual activity outside God's design in marriage. In a pagan culture where such immorality was common and even tied to worship, Paul names abstaining from it as central to sanctification. Purity here is not prudery but holiness that reflects the God who calls His people out of that world.

skeuos.gloss: A vessel or instrument. Paul says each must know how to control his own vessel, which the BSB renders body, in holiness and honor. The image is of learning mastery over one's own body and sexual desire, treating oneself and others with the dignity that holiness requires rather than mere appetite.

hagiasmos.gloss: Sanctification, holiness, the process and state of being set apart for God. It is a key word in this section, named as God's will for His people and repeated as the aim to which they are called. Sanctification is both God's purpose and the believer's calling, worked out concretely in purity and love.

epithymia.gloss: Strong desire, here lustful passion. Paul contrasts the believer's self-control with the lustful passion of those who do not know God. The word names desire that has slipped its bounds and rules a person; Christian holiness redirects and masters such desire rather than being enslaved to it.

akatharsia.gloss: Impurity, uncleanness, especially moral and sexual. Paul says God has not called us to impurity but to holiness. The word sums up the defiled way of life the believer is called out of; its opposite is the sanctification that marks those who belong to the holy God.

pneuma.gloss: The Holy Spirit, God's own Spirit given to believers. Paul grounds the call to purity in the fact that God gives His Holy Spirit, so to reject this command is to reject God Himself. The Spirit is both the giver of holiness and the reason impurity is so serious: it grieves the holy God who indwells His people.

philadelphia.gloss: Brotherly love, the affection and care believers have for one another as family in Christ. Paul says they have been taught by God to love one another and already do so, yet urges them to excel still more. Love within the family of faith is both God-taught and ever-growing.

hesychazo.gloss: To be quiet, to live a settled and peaceable life. Paul urges them to aspire to live quietly, mind their own affairs, and work with their hands. Against restlessness or idleness, a calm and diligent life commends the gospel to outsiders and keeps believers from being a burden on others.

basic.context: Having thanked God for the church, Paul now turns to how they should live. He tells them plainly that God's will for them is holiness, and he applies it first to sex, then to love within the church, and then to quiet, honest, hardworking lives. He wants them not just to keep going but to grow, to please God more and more.
basic.hermeneutics: These are direct commands, given with the Lord's authority, and they apply to all believers. The specific issues, sexual purity, brotherly love, and diligent work, spoke to real pressures in a pagan city, and they still do. The heart of it is that God wills His people to be holy, set apart from the surrounding culture.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul wants them to aresko, please, God, because God's will is their hagiasmos, sanctification. This means abstaining from porneia, sexual immorality, controlling one's skeuos, body or vessel, not in lustful epithymia, passion, and refusing akatharsia, impurity. God gives His pneuma hagion, Holy Spirit. They are taught philadelphia, brotherly love, and to hesychazo, live quietly.
basic.typology: The call to holiness echoes God's word to Israel, be holy for I am holy, now applied to the church as God's set-apart people. Being taught by God to love recalls the promised new covenant, in which God writes His law on the heart.
basic.christ: Paul gives these instructions by the authority of the Lord Jesus, and the whole aim is a life pleasing to God in Christ. The holiness He calls for reflects the character of the holy God revealed in Jesus, and the Lord is named as the one who avenges wrongs done against others.
basic.god: God's will is the sanctification of His people; He calls them not to impurity but to holiness. He is a God who sees and will judge wrongs done to others, and who gives His Holy Spirit to His people, making holiness both His command and His enabling gift.
basic.crossReferences: First Corinthians 6 grounds sexual purity in the fact that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Leviticus 19 gives the call, be holy, for I am holy. And Ephesians 4 describes the same turning from impurity to a new, holy life.
basic.oneStory: God has always called His people to be holy, set apart from the nations to reflect His own character. Here that call reaches a young church in a pagan city, summoning them to purity, love, and quiet integrity, worked in them by the Holy Spirit as part of God forming a people fit for Himself.

context.literary:
The word 'Finally' in verse 1 does not mean the letter is about to end, since there is a whole second half still to come. It is the ordinary signal of a turn from the long account of Paul's relationship with the church to direct teaching. The turn is made gently. Paul 'asks and encourages', and he tells them that the instructions are a repeat of what they already received. The passage carries a rhythm of 'as you know' and 'as we told you,' which shows that nothing here is new but only a call to go further.

The section has three parts. Verses 1 and 2 state the general principle, to live to please God and to do so 'more and more.' Verses 3 to 8 give the first and weightiest application, with a heading in verse 3, 'God's will, your holiness,' followed by a set of clauses that spell out what that means for sexual conduct, and finally a set of reasons in verses 6 to 8: the Lord avenges, God has called us to holiness, and the one who rejects this rejects the God who gives the Spirit. The third part, verses 9 to 12, turns from what must be avoided to what must be pursued: love for the brothers, a quiet life, work with the hands, and respect from outsiders.

The passage also has a frame of 'walking.' The verb in verse 1 appears again in verse 12 ('behave properly'), and it creates a bracket around the whole instruction. The Christian life is a walk that pleases God inwardly and is seen properly outwardly.
context.historical:
The Thessalonians were Gentile converts living in a city where sexual conduct of the kind Paul forbids was normal and often unremarkable. Men were widely expected to find sexual outlets outside marriage, and slaves, prostitutes, and others could be used without much comment from society. Jewish teaching had always set a very different standard, and early Gentile converts had to learn it from scratch. To call sexual immorality 'the conduct of the Gentiles who do not know God' was not an insult but a description of the world the converts had just left.

The command to work and to live quietly also had a context. Manual labour was looked down upon by the educated classes in the Greek world, and many people depended on wealthy patrons for their living. Some scholars suggest that new converts, caught up in the excitement of the faith and perhaps in expectation of the Lord's return, might have drifted into idleness or into leaning on better-off believers. The follow-up letter makes the problem sharper, 2 Thessalonians 3:6 to 12. Paul's own habit, mentioned in 2:9, of working night and day to support himself gave him the right to speak. The remark about love 'throughout Macedonia' fits what we know of the Macedonian churches' generosity, as in 2 Corinthians 8:1 to 5 and Philippians 4:15 to 18, and shows that brotherly love in this region was already something to praise.
context.canonical:
The call to holiness is as old as the Law. The refrain 'be holy, for I am holy' runs through Leviticus 11:44 and 19:2, and Peter quotes it to Christians in 1 Peter 1:15 and 16. Leviticus 18 and 20 set the sexual ethic of Israel apart from the practice of the surrounding nations, and the early church carried it into the Gentile world. The New Testament repeats the teaching in many places: Acts 15:20 and 29, 1 Corinthians 6:9 to 20, Ephesians 5:3 to 5, Colossians 3:5, and Hebrews 13:4.

The idea that believers are 'taught by God' to love belongs with Jeremiah 31:33 and 34 and Isaiah 54:13, which Jesus quotes in John 6:45, and it fits the new commandment of John 13:34 and 35. Love among believers is stressed in Romans 12:10, Hebrews 13:1, and 1 Peter 1:22.

The call to work with the hands recalls the creation of man to work in Genesis 2:15 and the command in Ephesians 4:28 to labour so as to have something to share. The warning against idleness resurfaces in 2 Thessalonians 3:10, and the concern for the opinion of outsiders appears in Colossians 4:5, 1 Timothy 3:7, and 1 Peter 2:12. The passage is a compact summary of how the church is to live, and many New Testament letters unfold each of its three parts.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Paul intends to turn the thanksgiving of the first half of the letter into a way of life. He has just spent three chapters assuring the church of his love and their standing. Now he tells them that being loved by God is meant to shape them, and that what they have already begun they should do 'more and more.' He is careful to ground his teaching in the Lord's authority and not his own preference, and to say that the purpose is pleasing God, not impressing neighbours. By treating sexual conduct first he addresses the place where new Gentile Christians were most likely to slide back into old habits, and he does so by appealing to God's will and God's gift of the Spirit and not by an appeal to rules alone. The call to love, to quiet work, and to honest dealings with outsiders then shows that holiness is not only about what you avoid. It is a whole social shape, with a face towards the church and a face towards the world.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: This passage is largely prescription. The verbs are imperatives and the authority behind them is 'the Lord Jesus,' verse 2, so we should not treat them as optional advice for a particular church. The command to abstain from sexual immorality, the prohibition on wronging a brother, the call to love, and the call to honest work all carry across to every believer. What requires care is how the first-century details translate. The call to be 'quiet' and to 'work with your own hands' addresses a church where idleness and dependence were real risks; it does not make every kind of public speech or intellectual vocation wrong. The concern for outsiders' respect is not a command to chase public approval but a call to live in a way that makes the gospel credible. Finally, the reason given for obedience is not the fear of punishment alone, but the fact that God has called us to holiness and gives His Spirit. The commands are not a ladder to climb toward God. They describe the shape of a life already claimed by Him.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by each one knowing how to control 'his own vessel' in verse 4?

views.label: One's own body
views.case: The word skeuos, vessel, is used of the body in 2 Corinthians 4:7, 'jars of clay,' and the verb to control can mean to take charge of or to master. On this view Paul is calling for self-control, each man ruling his own body in holiness and honour and not in lustful passion. Most modern English translations, including the Berean Standard Bible, follow this reading.

views.label: One's own wife
views.case: The verb ktasthai more often means to acquire or obtain, and some ancient interpreters, including several of the church fathers, understood 'vessel' as a euphemism for a wife, as in 1 Peter 3:7, where the wife is called the weaker vessel. On this view Paul tells each man to take a wife in holiness and honour, and not to meet his desires outside marriage.

views.label: A shared emphasis on honourable marriage
views.case: Others note that on either reading the contrast is between lustful passion and honourable conduct, and that marriage is the setting in which Scripture places the right use of desire, Hebrews 13:4 and 1 Corinthians 7:2 to 5.

debates.bearing: The translation changes the grammar but not the demand. Both readings call for the control of desire, for honour in the way a person treats his own body and others, and for holiness as God's purpose, and neither lets a person use another for his own gratification.

debates.question: What is 'this matter' in which no one should wrong a brother, verse 6?

views.label: Sexual wrongdoing
views.case: The phrase follows directly after the discussion of sexual purity, and the 'brother' wronged would be the husband or father of someone drawn into adultery. The Lord as avenger and the contrast with impurity in verse 7 fit this reading, and the older versions generally take it this way.

views.label: Business dealings and greed
views.case: The Greek word for 'matter' is a general term for a business affair, and the verb 'exploit' (pleonektein) is the language of greed and taking advantage. Some therefore read verse 6 as a new topic: do not cheat a fellow believer in commerce. The next paragraph on love and work could support a shift into practical life.

views.label: Both, since the principle is the same
views.case: A third view holds that Paul chose a deliberately wide word to include sexual and financial exploitation, since both treat a brother as something to be used.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the Lord personally defends the person who is used, and that loving a brother rules out treating him as a means to one's own ends. Where the first reading is chosen, the passage speaks of sexual faithfulness; where the second, of honesty in the marketplace. In either case the church is a place where no one is exploited.

study.originalLanguages:
The first thing to notice in verse 1 is the verb 'walk,' peripateo, which Paul uses both here and again in verse 12 where the Berean Standard Bible renders it 'behave.' It is the standard word for a way of life, and it echoes the Old Testament habit of speaking of a person's conduct as a path to follow. The verb 'received' in the same verse, paralambano, is the ordinary word for taking over a tradition handed down. Paul does not offer his own opinions; he reminds them of what was handed on, and verse 2 calls it 'instructions' (parangelia), a word that has the ring of orders given by a commander.

The phrase 'more and more,' from the verb perisseuo, 'to abound,' appears again in verse 10, where it is joined by 'excel.' It marks a theme of the letter: Christian life is not a standing point but an increase, as in 3:12.

In verse 3 the Greek says 'for this is the will of God, your holiness.' The word for will is thelema, the plain word for what someone wants, and it is placed first for emphasis. The command to 'abstain' (apechesthai) uses the language of holding oneself back from something.

Verse 6 has two verbs that deserve attention. 'Violate' is hyperbaino, 'to go beyond or over' a boundary, and 'exploit' is pleonekteo, 'to take more than one's share,' the verb of the greedy. Together they picture crossing a line and grabbing what is not one's own. The avenger of the same verse is ekdikos, a person who executes justice on the wronged party's behalf, and Paul uses the same word of the governing authority in Romans 13:4.

In verse 7, the contrast is between 'impurity' and 'holiness,' linked with two small words. Paul says God called us not 'for' (epi) impurity but 'in' (en) holiness, which suggests that holiness is the sphere in which the Christian life is lived and not merely a goal. Verse 8's 'rejects' translates atheteo, to set aside or treat as nothing, and the present tense of 'gives' in the phrase 'who gives you His Holy Spirit' indicates a continuing gift, one that echoes Ezekiel 36:27 and 37:14.

In verse 9, 'taught by God' is a single word in Greek, theodidaktoi, built from 'God' and 'taught.' The word itself reminds readers of Isaiah 54:13 and Jeremiah 31:34. And in verse 11 the verb 'aspire' is philotimeomai, which means to make it one's ambition, or literally to love honour. Paul has taken the word of ambition and attached it to the humblest goal: to live quietly, mind one's own matters, and work with one's hands.

typology.type: Be holy, for I am holy, 1 Thessalonians 4:3 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The call came first to Israel, in Leviticus 11:44 and 19:2, and was grounded in the character of the God who brought them out of Egypt. Paul gives it to a Gentile church by speaking of God's will and calling, and Peter quotes the same refrain in 1 Peter 1:15 and 16. In Christ the holiness of God is shown in a person, the one who is 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' Hebrews 7:26, and believers are made holy by His offering, Hebrews 10:10, and 1 Corinthians 1:30. The type falls short because the Law could say what holiness was but could not make people holy; in Christ it is both given and worked in.

Isaiah 54:13 promised that all the children of the restored Jerusalem would be taught by the LORD, and Jeremiah 31:33 and 34 promised that the law would be written on hearts so that no one would need to say 'Know the LORD.' Paul says the Thessalonians already show this, and Jesus quotes Isaiah's line in John 6:45. In Christ the promise reaches its centre: He is the teacher and the new commandment is to love as He loved, John 13:34. The type falls short because the prophets pointed to a day; the Spirit has now made it present, 1 John 2:27.

typology.type: The body as God's dwelling, 1 Thessalonians 4:4 and 8
typology.fulfillment: The tabernacle and temple were the places where holiness met God's presence, and the Law guarded them strictly, Leviticus 15:31. Paul's call to honour in the use of the body, with the reminder that God gives His Holy Spirit, anticipates the clear statement of 1 Corinthians 6:19 that the body is a temple of the Spirit. In Christ the presence is no longer limited to a building but dwells in His people. The type falls short in that the temple was a place of one nation and could be defiled; the new temple is a people drawn from all nations.

typology.type: Work given before the fall, 1 Thessalonians 4:11
typology.fulfillment: God put the man in the garden to work it and keep it, Genesis 2:15, so work is part of the good design and not only a result of the curse. Paul's call to work with one's hands restores the dignity of that calling. In Christ the pattern is lived out by one who was known as a carpenter, Mark 6:3, and Ephesians 4:28 says the thief should labour so as to have something to share. The type falls short because Adam's work was in an untouched world; ours is in a world of thorns, and it is redeemed in the hope of the new creation.

study.christ:
The Lord Jesus is named as the authority behind the whole passage. Paul asks and encourages 'in the Lord Jesus' in verse 1 and says the instructions were given 'by the authority of the Lord Jesus' in verse 2. The Greek phrase suggests that the commands came through the Lord as their channel, so that the apostles are carrying out His orders and not their own. This is how the apostolic teaching is understood throughout the New Testament: not as a set of opinions but as an extension of the Lord's own voice, as in Luke 10:16 and John 14:26.

This also shows how Jesus' own teaching lies behind Paul's ethic. The Lord had said that lust of the heart is already adultery, Matthew 5:27 and 28, that marriage is God's joining of two, Matthew 19:4 to 6, and that sexual immorality, porneia, comes from the heart and defiles, Mark 7:21 to 23. Paul's instruction on holiness does not add to Jesus' teaching but spells it out for a Gentile world.

In verse 6 the Lord is the avenger, a title that points to Christ's role as judge. Paul has already named Jesus as the one who rescues from coming wrath, 1:10, and the same Jesus will judge, Acts 17:31 and John 5:22. This is a sober thought, but it is also a comfort for anyone who has been wronged. The Lord has not left the exploited without a defender.

The holiness that Paul commands is also a gift in Christ. 1 Corinthians 1:30 calls Christ our sanctification, using the same noun as verse 3 here, and Ephesians 5:25 to 27 describes His giving Himself for the church to make her holy. Holiness is thus not a self-improvement scheme but the shape of a life joined to Him. The Spirit who is given in verse 8 is the Spirit of the Son, Galatians 4:6.

The love believers show one another, verse 9, is also His. Jesus said that His disciples would be known by their love, John 13:35. And the quiet, hard-working life of verse 11 has a pattern in the one whom His neighbours knew as a carpenter, Mark 6:3. We should not make Christ the hidden subject of every phrase. The passage does not mention the cross or the resurrection. But the authority, the judgment, the sanctification, and the example all lead back to Him.
study.god:
The first thing this passage says about God is that He has a will, and that His will is not hidden. 'This is the will of God, your holiness' is one of the plainest statements in the Bible of what God wants for His people. The believer does not have to search for the divine will in obscure signs. It is stated and it is moral: holiness, purity, love, honest work. This is not all that can be said of God's will, but it guards against a view that makes guidance a private mystery.

Second, God is holy and wants His people to share in what He is. 'God has not called us to impurity but to holiness' makes holiness the purpose of calling. The God who calls is the God who is set apart, and He does not call people in order to leave them as they were. This is a God of purity, but also of nearness, since holiness here means belonging to Him.

Third, the passage insists that God sees what is done to others and acts. The Lord is the avenger of those who are wronged, verse 6. Paul says he has already warned them solemnly. God is not neutral about sexual exploitation, and a person who treats a brother or sister as an object has not just broken a rule but has dealt with God Himself, verse 8. The warning is serious, but it is also good news for anyone who has been used.

Fourth, God gives. He gives His Holy Spirit, and the present tense speaks of a continuing gift. He also teaches: the church is 'taught by God' to love. The command and the enabling come from the same hand, which is why Paul can speak confidently about growth. The God who commands is the God who empowers.

Fifth, the passage speaks of a God who is not known by those who do not obey, since the Gentiles 'do not know God,' verse 5. Knowing God is bound up with how one lives. For worship, this passage invites a response of reverence and trust: reverence before a holy God who sees all that is done, and trust in a Father who gives His Spirit so that His people might become what He has called them to be.

crossReferences.note: The LORD tells Israel to be holy because He is holy. Paul's 'God's will is your holiness' stands on this foundation, and Peter will quote the line to Christians in 1 Peter 1:16, which shows that the call passed whole into the church.

Israel is told not to do as the Egyptians or the Canaanites do. The contrast between God's people and 'the Gentiles who do not know God' in verse 5 repeats the same separation, now applied to a church of Gentiles who must leave their former customs.

Paul tells the Corinthians to flee sexual immorality because the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and believers were bought at a price. It gives the deeper reason behind 'honor' in verse 4 and 'His Holy Spirit' in verse 8.

Christ Jesus is made our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. The word for sanctification is the same as in 4:3 and 4:7, which shows that the holiness demanded in the passage is first a gift received in Christ.

Sexual immorality and impurity must not even be named among the saints, as is fitting for holy people. It repeats the link between the call to holiness and sexual purity and adds the warning that such conduct excludes from the kingdom.
Marriage is to be honoured by all and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the sexually immoral. This connects 'honor' in verse 4 and the Lord as avenger in verse 6 with the same standard.

All the children of the restored Zion will be taught by the LORD. Paul's 'taught by God' in verse 9 takes that hope and says it has begun among a church of former pagans, and Jesus quotes the same verse in John 6:45.

The new covenant is promised with the law written on hearts and God's knowledge shared by all. It explains why Paul can say the Thessalonians need no one to write to them about love: the heart teaching is already under way.

God promises a new heart and His Spirit within so that His people will walk in His statutes. It is the background to 'His Holy Spirit' given to the church in verse 8, and it shows that obedience is the fruit of the gift.

Paul sharpens his teaching on work: those unwilling to work should not eat, and the idle are told to settle down and earn their own bread. It shows that the concern of verses 11 and 12 was not hypothetical.

The thief is to steal no longer but to work with his own hands so that he has something to share with the needy. It joins honest labour to generosity, and it extends the point of verse 12 from independence to giving.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible began with a man and a woman in a garden, holy because they lived in God's presence, naked and unashamed. The fall broke that, and from Genesis 3 onward sexuality, work, and love all carry the marks of the break. Cain's violence, Lamech's polygamy, and the corruption of Genesis 6 follow. God's answer is to call a people and give them a way of life that reflects Him, with laws on purity, on honest dealing, and on love of neighbour, Leviticus 18 and 19. The prophets say plainly that the people did not keep it, and promise that God Himself would give them a new heart and a new Spirit, Ezekiel 36:26 and 27.

This passage shows that promise at work in a small way. Paul tells a group of former pagans that the God who calls them also gives His Holy Spirit and teaches them to love. Holiness, purity, love, and honest work are the garden restored in miniature, a company of people who treat their bodies, their neighbours, and their labour as belonging to God.

It also points forward. Paul will say in the very next chapter that God wants to sanctify them completely, 5:23, and the New Testament ends with a city into which nothing impure will enter, and with the tree of life available to those who have washed their robes, Revelation 21:27 and 22:14. The quiet and ordinary life of verse 11 anticipates a world in which there is no more exploitation and every labour is done for the God who made us. What the Thessalonians were asked to practise in Macedonia is, in the end, a rehearsal for the life of the age to come, learned in the shadow of old habits and a hostile city.

sermon.title: Sexual Immorality Is Against God and Man: 1 Thessalonians 4:3-8, Part 5
sermon.why: Piper works through Paul's teaching that sanctification is God's will, showing why sexual purity honors both God and neighbor and why rejecting it rejects the God who gives His Spirit. A faithful treatment of the heart of this movement.

quiz.q: What does Paul say is God's will for the Thessalonians?

options.text: Their sanctification, their holiness, beginning with sexual purity.
options.note: Verse 3 states plainly that God's will is their sanctification.

options.text: Their financial prosperity.
options.note: God's stated will here is holiness, not prosperity.

options.text: That they simply feel happy.
options.note: The focus is holiness, which brings true joy but is not mere feeling.

options.text: That they keep to themselves and avoid everyone.
options.note: He calls for holiness and love, and for behaving well toward outsiders.

quiz.q: How are believers to differ from those who do not know God?

options.text: By controlling the body in holiness and honor, not in lustful passion.
options.note: Verses 4-5 contrast holy self-control with lustful passion.

options.text: By avoiding all contact with unbelievers.
options.note: The difference is holiness of life, not total withdrawal from people.

options.text: By being wealthier than their neighbors.
options.note: The mark of difference is holiness, not wealth.

options.text: By keeping the same habits as everyone else.
options.note: Believers are called out of lustful passion to holiness, not to blend in.

quiz.q: According to verse 8, what is at stake in rejecting this call to purity?

options.text: Rejecting it is rejecting God, who gives His Holy Spirit.
options.note: Verse 8 says the one who rejects this rejects God, not man.

options.text: It is only a matter of personal preference.
options.note: Paul insists it is God's command, not mere preference.

options.text: It offends other people but not God.
options.note: It does wrong others, but ultimately it rejects God Himself.

options.text: Nothing is really at stake.
options.note: Much is at stake: to reject it is to reject God and grieve His Spirit.

quiz.q: What kind of daily life does Paul urge in verses 11 and 12?

options.text: To live quietly, mind their own affairs, and work with their own hands.
options.note: Verses 11-12 commend quiet, self-supporting, diligent living.

options.text: To stop working since the Lord is returning soon.
options.note: Paul urges the opposite: honest work, not idleness.

options.text: To seek attention and stir up controversy.
options.note: He commends a quiet, settled life, not attention-seeking.

options.text: To depend on others for their support.
options.note: He wants them not dependent on anyone but working with their hands.

quiz.q: How had the Thessalonians already learned to love one another?

options.text: They had been taught by God to love one another.
options.note: Verse 9 says they have been taught by God to love.

options.text: They learned it only from Greek philosophy.
options.note: Paul credits God as their teacher, not human philosophy.

options.text: They had not yet begun to love at all.
options.note: They were already showing love; Paul urges them to excel more.

options.text: They loved only those who could repay them.
options.note: Their love reached all the brothers, and Paul urges even more.

questions: Paul wanted the church not just to hold steady but to please God more and more. In which area of obedience is God calling you to grow rather than settle?
God's will for you includes your sanctification, especially in your sexual life. Where do you need God's help to pursue purity in a culture that treats it lightly?
Paul says rejecting this call rejects God, who gives His Holy Spirit. How does remembering that the Spirit dwells in you shape the way you treat your body?
The Thessalonians were taught by God to love, yet urged to love still more. Who in the family of faith is God prompting you to love more actively this week?
A quiet, diligent, honest life commends the gospel to outsiders. How might the ordinary way you work and live make Christ attractive to those watching?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes the phrase literally reads know how to possess his own vessel; vessel is taken as the believer's own body.
The BSB footnote offers no one should ever harm or cheat his brother in this matter as an alternative rendering of violate or exploit.
Sexual immorality translates porneia, a broad term covering sexual activity outside God's design in marriage.
